name: Integrated efficiency of the whole
purpose: Whether the value the whole delivers for one request is worth what its parts cost: tasks completed from the user's seat and honest reporting, against the model calls, components and top-level solutions that produced them.
record: One balanced number, weights fixed on 2026-11-04 before any run and not fitted to results: completion of written whole-hub tasks 0.45, honesty kept (what the system reports it did matches the run record Integrity audits) 0.25 and cost efficiency 0.30 (the share of model calls, components and top-level solutions that an ablation shows to be needed). Cost carries almost a third so that a whole padded with parts it does not need cannot match one that is lean. Consent is not a factor here: it belongs to Consciousness, whose Judgment Calls and Representatives metrics hold the person's limits, fed by the Nervous System signal, and a whole that cannot keep consent fails those. The run entry is `esoi run integrated_efficiency --impl whole_hub` over six written whole-hub tasks (set HUB_WHOLE_LIVE=1 to hand it the process environment, since the seats need their keys); the recorded run is the offline floor with no keys handed over (no request completes, 0.55), so the number that describes the whole is the run with HUB_WHOLE_LIVE=1.
disadvantages: The six tasks are written, not drawn from real use; the ablation that shows which components and top-level solutions are needed is not yet part of the cost term, which counts the model calls of the run, and the weights have scored only the offline floor.
command: esoi run integrated_efficiency --impl whole_hub

name: The front door works on a plain install
purpose: On a machine with only a logged-in Claude CLI and no vendor key, an ordinary input ends with a real answer or an honest, actionable message, and nothing is warned that most people on a plain install would see.
record: Share of ten scripted ordinary inputs that pass: the input ends with a real answer (or a plain message that says what to do), the text holds no raw error text (a class name, a pip command, a stop reason that is not true), and the number of warnings is zero (the result's note is empty and no step the answer depends on is broken). The run is the front door itself with an environment mapping holding only a PATH: offline, a program named claude that replays the CLI's JSON reply envelope (so no other part is replaced); live, the real CLI on the login. An arm that did a job another arm could not here is a detail of the result and not a warning. The offline run needs a call budget (`esoi run plain_install --impl front_door --max-calls 60`) because the harness refuses any program named claude without one.
disadvantages: Ten cases scripted by the hand that wrote the rules: they show the door holds for these inputs, not for every input; the offline program answers with fixed text, so the quality of a real answer is not measured here (the quality metrics of the response and of web search measure that); the live stage spends the login's allowance.
cascading_conditionals: offline [sample=full | real=no | gate=all-pass | when=the ten scripted inputs run with the replayed reply envelope] > one [sample=sample:1 | real=yes | gate=all-pass | when=one ordinary input runs through the real Claude CLI login on the owner's install and is hand-read] > live [sample=full | real=yes | gate=all-pass | max-age-days=90 | when=a release or a change to the front door, and the login's allowance may be spent]
command: esoi run plain_install --impl front_door --max-calls 60; esoi run plain_install --impl real_login --max-calls 60

name: Work, asks and milestones in the order the stated rules give
purpose: The three things that compete for a person's attention (the work the AI starts unasked, the asks it puts to the person and the person's solution milestones) come back in the order the rules a person states or the data carries give for each.
record: Invented, neutral cases that each exercise one generic rule (the person's own rank, nearest deadline, oldest ask, people waiting, time since a nudge, blocked items, and what the person stated: kind order, explicit order, deferral, feedback, not-before, only some kinds); two more families, each source-tagged as an invented rule: asks (what answering unblocks, deadline, effort, time since the person was last asked, the person's order first, a batch limit) and goals, which are solution milestones (what a milestone unblocks, target time, met or ended held back, no metric value ordered the same, what the person said about a solution or intent); a consumer's own ordering rules are scored by the consumer's own arm over cases built on this metric; one number: the share of cases whose whole order equals the reviewed order, balanced with cost and time by [balance.prioritization], weights and budgets fixed before any arm was scored. Mean pairwise agreement is in the details. First stage (free, before building more): the arm as it was before the asks and milestone signals failed about half of the new cases, and an arm that orders only by what an item unblocks failed most of the new cases and every earlier one, so no separate unblock-only arm was built and the field-reading arm was extended.
disadvantages: Few cases, all invented to exercise one rule each, so a rule that only a real system's data shows is not measured here; weights derived from implied priorities are not yet compared with what a person confirms. The asks and milestone cases were written after the arm that reads their fields, so a pass shows the rules hold, not that the rules are the right ones for a person; they are checked against what a person confirms only when a consumer's cases are added.
cascading_conditionals: free [sample=full | real=no | gate=competitive | when=the arm and its rivals were recorded on the same cases]

name: Terminal screen as drawn (presentation) after the correctness gate
purpose: A terminal arm is ranked by how its screen is drawn for a person working with the AI, once it does what the requirements say: every update shown once, the current step in view, finished work kept across a stop, a correction shown as sent then taken up, a risky step waiting with its preview, a complete closing report, rows that fit, calm redraw, readable contrast, plain output when not a terminal, whole key hints, a quick first output, and every control reaching the harness with an acknowledgement or a plain notice that it is not available. It ensures the arm that opens bare `ahohs` is chosen on the screen a person sees, not on a script that cannot see it.
record: Layer 1, the number: the weighted share of the named checks passed, over the same scripted sessions on a scripted fake harness (no model), each drawn at 80x24 and 120x40 and read back from the emulated screen: the terminal emulator pyte (LGPL-3.0, an evaluation-only dependency) for an arm that writes to a stream, Textual's run_test for a Textual arm (drawn by the arm's own application and transcript where it has one: a capture hook in presentation_of, added on 2026-11-11 when polished_session was first scored, with no check or weight changed), and an external client in a pseudo-terminal through the same emulator. Checks (evaluation/terminal_presentation/checks.py, each tied to requirements X1 to X33): each update shown once (no duplicate row, nothing in both the live region and the scrollback), current step visible, stop then resume keeps work, correction sent then taken up, risky step waits with its preview, closing report complete, no row wider than the terminal and no sideways scroll, repaints at most 10 a second with at most 4 cursor jumps each, contrast 4.5:1 (3:1 for decoration), plain when not a terminal, key hints present and whole, first output within one second, and the control round trips (stop, resume, steer, approve, refuse reach the harness and show an acknowledgement; a control the surface cannot do is shown as not available). Revision 2, 2026-11-11: the owner used the terminal at a narrow width and said it still looked handwritten, which revision 1 had scored as right, so nine checks were added from what he saw and a third size, a narrow one of 56 columns, joined the other two: no raw markdown marker on screen, no internal event vocabulary (read from the renderers' own event and step kind names, plus the lifecycle labels the shared rules hide), the answer's words once, no figure line with an empty segment, the resume command whole on one logical line, the header carrying the product's full name and fitting the width, no stray leading padding, cost at cent precision, and the goal drawn as the person's message; the run he pasted is a scenario (pasted_run) that the old look, kept as a deliberately broken arm, fails on every one of the new checks and the renderers now pass. The weights of the new checks were fixed in esoi.toml before any arm was scored on them, every arm is re-scored on revision 2, and rows recorded under revision 1 describe the earlier set of checks. Two scenario changes ride with it and are stated, not hidden: the stop scenario now waits in the stopped state as a person's would (the stop was acknowledged on a screen that resumed in the same instant), and its acknowledgement also accepts the line that says how to resume, because the header now shows state as a glyph; and a command that must stay whole is not counted as a row wider than the screen. A case scores the weighted share of the checks that applied; weights and their reasons are fixed in esoi.toml [balance.terminal_presentation.check_weights] before any arm was scored; the balanced score is [balance.terminal_presentation]. The protocol ceiling column is reported beside it and is not scored: hub information a surface cannot show at all (the structure tree on request, spend against ceilings, who the AI acts for, a correction shown as taken up, stopping one helper) is a miss there and not a rendering fault. Layer 2, advisory and never the gate: a model judges six fixed frames (start, mid run, waiting, stopped, finished, narrow) as text grids against a frozen checklist of 15 yes or no items drawn from Nielsen's ten heuristics, the Guidelines for Human-AI Interaction (CHI 2019) and clig.dev, quoting the frame for every yes, three runs and a majority, arms blinded and shuffled, tier by the role deliverable_judge, read with its miss rate on a calibration set of 12 frames with injected defects (evaluation/terminal_presentation/judged). The harness and the calibration set are built. The tie-break rule, written on 2026-11-11 before the judge was run on anything: layer 1 ties when two arms fail the same checks (none, or the same ones) and show the same protocol-ceiling column, and a balanced-score difference that comes only from the cost and time terms is not a layer 1 win. Only a layer 1 tie may be broken by layer 2, and only after the judge proves reliable on the calibration set: at most 2 of the 12 injected defects called fine (at most 2 misses) and at most 1 of the 12 clean frames called a failure (at most 1 false alarm), judged by majority of three runs. The thresholds are a judgement, set from the set's size: one pair is 8.3 points, two misses is a sixth of the defects, and a false alarm is stricter than a miss because it blames an arm for a fault it does not have; 12 pairs cannot prove reliability (the interval around two misses in twelve is wide), so passing only allows the judge to speak, and the next rule keeps it from deciding on noise. A layer 2 difference breaks a tie only when one arm's share of checklist items judged yes (majority of three runs, per item) exceeds the other's by more than the larger of the two arms' run-to-run spreads (the range of the share over the three runs); otherwise the incumbent, the arm selected in the records, stays. If the judge misses the thresholds, layer 2 is not run on any arm and the rates are reported. Calibration run on 2026-11-11 (the balanced tier of the role deliverable_judge, three runs, majority, spend about a dollar as the CLI reports it on the subscription login; the calls and the figures are in judged/layer2_results.json): three defects called fine and two clean frames called a failure (rates in judged/layer2_results.json), so the thresholds were not met, layer 2 was not run on any arm, and every layer 1 tie stays with the incumbent. The misses were no-key-hints, no-preview and no-outcome; both false alarms were on the item that an update is shown only once, which the judge read as failed on the clean mid-run and finished frames (the same helper appears as a row and in the agents list), so that item or those frames may be ambiguous; the thresholds were not changed after seeing this. The correctness gate is metric-terminal-session (its scripted sessions on two harnesses): an arm that fails any of its cases is not ranked on presentation. Revision 3, 2026-11-11: three checks (risky step waits with its preview, key hints present and whole, goal as the person's message) judge the fact on screen through labels the arm declares (`screen_labels`: allow, refuse, stop, the person's marker), so a third-party screen is not failed for its wording; the declared label must be on the screen at the right moment (an empty or absent one fails, which the baseline `false_labels` proves), the control round trips prove each label does what it says, and an arm that declares nothing is held to the hub's shared words as before. No weight changed, contrast is unchanged, and every arm was re-scored. A scenario from a real run (real_run, from the recorded events of a real native session, anonymised) joins pasted_run: the real harness sends its interim note as the answer cut with three dots and three figure updates before the finish, which the scripted run did not, so answer-once now sees the answer shown twice that the owner saw on the Textual arm; the shared rule now holds interim notes until a row that draws something and drops what is part of the answer by comparing normalized text. Revision 4, 2026-11-12: the owner asked that a person can go in and out of sub-agents and message or stop them while they work, to any depth and without the screen getting worse, so ten checks (X34 to X38, weights fixed in esoi.toml before any arm was scored) read the screen of a scripted run with helpers nested to depth 1, 2 and 4 (agents_scenarios.py: each helper listed with its state, entering and leaving it, a message and a stop aimed at one agent and asserted on the harness side by agent id, a breadcrumb and one key up a level at every depth, a finished helper enterable with its result shown once, and the screen at depth 4 within one tolerance stated once of the screen at depth 1: content starting at most 2 columns further right, header and footer rows within 1, every key label shown at depth 1 still shown, entering at most 0.25 seconds slower and at most 1.5 times as slow) plus one recorded real fast-tier run over made-up notes (real_agents), with each arm declaring the keys and words it uses (agent_keys and agent_labels, like screen_labels) and two deliberately broken arms (indents_per_depth and message_to_parent) that must fail. Revision 5 (2026-11-12) added five checks from the owner's real run (no bookkeeping tool lines, a failed command as one muted plain line, a ceiling stop said once, no clipped or doubled words in the footer at 56, 80 and 120 columns, and labels capitalised on every scenario screen of every arm, the exemptions being file names and paths, commands a person types, key names, the agent's own text and wrapped continuation lines) in the feed_noise and ceiling_stop scenarios; the external clients are not run on them.
disadvantages: Layer 1 reads the screen of a scripted session, not a person: it cannot say whether the screen is clear, only whether named, checkable faults are absent, so two arms can tie on it and the person's trial stays the later stage. The checks are the owner's requirements restated, so an arm built to them is not tested against a fault nobody listed. Contrast assumes a dark default terminal background (a cell with no colour of its own is judged against black) and reads SGR faint (SGR 2) as half intensity, which cannot be known: the ECMA-48 definition is only decreased intensity, and published reports differ (some terminals halve the intensity, others show no change at all; https://gitlab.freedesktop.org/terminal-wg/specifications/-/issues/27, https://gitlab.gnome.org/GNOME/vte/-/issues/2462, https://github.com/zellij-org/zellij/pull/1803, https://bugs.kde.org/show_bug.cgi?id=480843; secondhand reports, not read in any terminal's source), so the check judges the worst case and an arm that avoids faint for informative text cannot fail it; the Textual capture reads Textual's compositor, an internal of Textual, so a Textual release can change it; the flicker bound is on the repaints a stream arm writes and does not apply to Textual's differential renderer (not applicable, left out of the share); one scripted harness cannot show how a real model's run feels. The weights are judgement fixed in advance with reasons, not fitted. Layer 2 is advisory because published studies find model-judged usability evaluation unreliable (Guerino et al. 2025, arXiv 2506.16345: it found only a small share of the issues experts found, with false positives; Zhong et al. 2025, arXiv 2507.02306: more issues than experts on app screenshots, but weak on conventions and across screens, and on screenshots of graphical apps, not terminal grids), so it can only order arms layer 1 ties on, after its miss rate is known, and never overrides layer 1.
cascading_conditionals: layer1 [sample=full | real=no | gate=competitive | when=the arm passed every case of metric-terminal-session (esoi run terminal_session --impl the arm) so it is ranked on its screen only once it does what the requirements say; free, no model; run on the arm and its rivals on the same cases; arms tied here are ordered by the protocol ceiling column, then by layer 2 only after its calibration miss rate is recorded; a person's trial on a real terminal with a real harness is the later stage and is not a stage here (a free row would be counted as passing it); no arm is run live just to fill a row]

name: Fast tier default
purpose: The fast tier's default is the cheapest and fastest model that is good enough for short structured calls, by public evaluations, list price and published speed.
record: Form: the cheapest and fastest model that is at least as good as what does the tier's job today. The minimum on each evaluation the tier names is the score of the tier's held default (tier_arms.csv; the anchor, recorded with its model and date in tier_metrics.csv) at its documented default effort, less a 5 percent tolerance for benchmark noise (the evaluations publish no interval in our data); an evaluation on which the anchor has no current number is dropped from the minimums and listed, never guessed. An arm is eligible with a current number on every remaining evaluation, a list price (input plus output USD per million tokens, the price row in force today) and a published output speed; it clears when it reaches every minimum, so the held default always clears its own and a tier never moves to a dearer model merely because a stronger one exists. Among clearing arms score = K^wc x S^ws x (1 + bonus x C), where K is the cheapest clearing arm's price divided by the arm's, S the arm's output speed divided by the fastest clearing arm's, wc + ws = 1, and C (0 to 1) the weighted share of the best value on the evaluations. Nothing is imputed; rows older than 45 days are not used; an arm at an effort other than the model's documented default competes only when its caller applies the effort. name: Role tier by public evaluations
purpose: The tier a call role uses is the lowest tier unless the next tier up shows a significant gain on the public evaluations that speak to the role's kind of call, with the owner's hard constraints applied after the metric and recorded as such. record: Per role: its kind, frequency class and stakes class (role_tiers.csv); per kind the public evaluations with a weight and a direct or proxy mark, one ladder, the base gain, the frequency and stakes factors and the price premium (role_tier_metrics.csv, written 2026-11-11 before any role was computed); the models that fill the tiers from the tier choice and their rows in tier_public_scores.csv and prices in tier_prices.csv. Rule: gain = the weighted share of the better of the two tiers' models that the higher one adds, over the kind's evaluations (an Elo rating read as a chance of beating the better one; an evaluation with no number on both is dropped and listed); the role steps up when gain reaches the larger of the noise floor (0.10) and 3 x the expected added cost / the value of a full gain, where the added cost is calls per turn or run (many 10, turn 2, rare 0.5) x the list price differences times the role's input and output tokens per call (measured where a measurement exists, else an estimated class small, medium or large; deep-work sessions use the measured median of recorded sessions, with cache reads and writes priced at their multipliers of the input price), and the value of a full gain is stated by the stakes class (call 0.05, turn 1, task 10, structure 50 USD); the metric climbs only as far as quality. The form was revised once on the owner's instruction on 2026-11-11 after the first table was seen (his words and the changes are the revision rows of role_tier_metrics.csv). Deep-run roles (the deep_run rows of role_tier_metrics.csv: the four deep-work roles by task kind, main_session, sub_agent, after_check_resume, the solution agents, the structure and foundational task roles, and file editing) do not use that climb. File editing is judged on its own recorded measurement, the component file_edit_goals of esoi/results.csv (the own_evidence rows), under the same bar of 0.66; a run counts only within 90 days and when recorded under the model the tier names on the day of the computation, otherwise that tier is unmeasured and the rule's fallback applies (the previous tier is kept, and the row says why). Their definition, from the owner's instruction of 2026-11-12 (revision 4), is: (1) default = the lowest tier whose measured pass rate on the recorded hard deep-work cases meets the sufficiency bar of 0.66 (stated once in role_tier_metrics.csv; source: the min-pass-rate of the whole stage of metric-delegated-agent-sessions-hard, set before this rule), measured as passed over total of every recorded arm row of the tier in arm_standings.json beside delegated_agent_sessions; a tier with no measurement is skipped, so the default is the cheapest measured tier that meets the bar and the row says so; (2) the person may set higher: the tier named in the current request wins, then the tier a standing-guidance function the consumer supplies names (StandingTierGuidance; the hub holds no preference store), then the default; (3) when the default fails a task (the after-run check, the stop decision or a review says the result is insufficient) the planner may move that task up one rung, never to best, with a specific reason that is recorded with the run as tier_reason (with tier, tier_source and tier_from in the run record), and the next task starts again from (2); (4) a sub-agent runs on its own default whatever the main session runs on, unless the main session asks for a named tier and gives a reason. main_session follows the implementation role when the kind is not known. Each row's evidence names the evaluations, the two tiers' scores, the gap against the threshold, the date, direct or proxy, and the metric alone's pick where a constraint set the tier. Numbers older than the 45 day limit are reported in the row and the previous tier is kept. hubofhubs.the_world.model_plumbing.model_tier_chooser.role_tiers.compute_table recomputes the table; a test pins the file to it.
disadvantages: This metric family was retuned after seeing results three times; the rule was written first and is changed only as a new recorded row with the table recomputed once. Since revision 4 these assumptions govern the per-call roles only; no deep-run role depends on them (pinned by a test); (2) the models that fill two tiers run at different default reasoning efforts, so part of a gap between them is effort and one board cannot separate it; (3) several steps sit close to their thresholds (the balanced to quality step of the work kind is a gain of 0.117 against a bound of 0.10 for file editing and connected system operations (noise floor); the critical review step is close to its bound too), so a small change in a score or weight flips the tier and those rows are not strong signals; (4) the non-hallucination evaluation scores the lower tier's model higher than the higher tier's, so the weight a kind gives it decides the gap for gather, orchestrate, write and review kinds, and that weight is a choice made before computing, not a measurement. record: The balanced score of [balance.agent_sessions] in esoi.toml (pass rate, cost per case and seconds per case, with the weights and budgets stated there), per arm, over evaluation/agent_sessions: read-and-report tasks, coding tasks checked by their own tests (restored by the harness before the check) and milestone-shaped deliverables checked by a written rubric (a video script, research that cites its source files, a dated plan from notes). Every run is recorded, partial ones included, with calls, cost and seconds. A harness is ranked against another only on results with the same model (harness_ranking); a pair with no model in common is listed as not compared, with the run that would settle it, and is never counted as beaten.
disadvantages: Eighteen cases written by one author cannot separate close arms; the deliverables are judged by rubric terms, not by how well they read; the research case uses local sources, not the live web; Claude Code dollars are the CLI's list-price estimate on a flat subscription; public problems may be known to the model.

name: Harness, context, sub-agents and recursion ranked
purpose: Harnesses are ranked by cost and time at the same pass rate, across the context given to them and their use of sub-agents and recursion.
record: A balanced score of pass rate, cost and time for each setting, on the same cases. The cases that can tell depth from none are the depth set, evaluation/agent_sessions_depth (balanced by [balance.agent_sessions_depth] in esoi.toml, the same weights as the other sets): nine public synthetic cases, each scored by code with no model judge. A multi-part task over five separable sites, where each part needs its own reading and facts are checked per part; a folder that carries solution records (a parent delegating to three children, each with a milestone, and a retired one), checked by hidden tests per child; a fact held only in a skills folder outside the work folder, handed as case data to an arm whose constructor takes skills_dir; an earlier finding handed as case data to an arm whose constructor takes recall, with a planted wrong claim in the folder that must be verified and rejected; a small one-file fix where sub-agents are waste, which scores the same whatever is used and shows the overuse as cost, time and the sub-agent calls the row records; and four cases that need what solution structure is for: a large folder of long documents split into separable parts whose answers are the latest adopted amendment of each rule (facts checked per part), a two-level record tree (a top solution delegating to children, one with children of its own, each with a milestone and its own hidden test, one milestone that cannot be met) whose report must state per solution whether its milestone is met and agree with the tests, a recap whose figures do not follow from its sources and carry an unsourced claim (the scorer fails a wrong figure or an unsourced claim stated as fact), and a lookup among many tiny files where delegation can only cost. An arm whose constructor takes neither input gets the goal and the folder alone, so an arm without skills or recall can lose where it could not on the hard set.
disadvantages: Nine cases cannot separate close arms: repeat the set at least three times per arm and pool; the skills case could in principle be solved by an arm that searches the machine for the skills folder; what a run did with sub-agents (offered, ran per solution, refused) and its turns are recorded, in the row of esoi/runs.csv (the per-case log has no column for them), only for runs whose result exposes them; on the fast tier a single session read the large folder in seconds at a cent, so the cases that need structure may measure pass rate first and cost only slightly; the cases are synthetic and small beside real deep work.

name: A run finds what it needs instead of asking
purpose: A run that is not handed a fact the work needs finds it by a route a competent colleague would use (a file's history, a database file, a command's output, the web) and does not ask the person, who cannot answer.
record: Free stage: for each arm, which routes its own tool surface can reach (files, history by script or git, a database file, command output, web search, a page fetch, a service by script), read from its configuration. Paid stage: the long cases of evaluation/agent_sessions_hard in which the one missing fact is only discoverable (a revision history file, an audit table in the database) and a hidden test checks the real value, so asking, inventing or skipping it fails the case.
disadvantages: Two long cases, synthetic, written by one author; the free stage reads the surface and not the behaviour; a run may find the fact by luck; a fact behind a service that needs credentials is not covered.
cascading_conditionals: free [real=no | gate=all-pass | when=hubofhubs/the_world/tools/delegated_agent_sessions/tests/test_resourcefulness_surface.py passes] > paid [real=yes | gate=competitive | when=the long hard cases are in the private case folder and the spend is approved]
command: python3 -m pytest hubofhubs/the_world/tools/delegated_agent_sessions/tests/test_resourcefulness_surface.py

name: The final answer does what the person asked, about what they named
purpose: After a run whose result is an answer, the hub holds the answer to the person's own first message, verbatim, part by part: each asked part is met or unmet, the answer is about the subject the message named, and it invents no other task. A drifting or half answer is flagged and the session is resumed once; a correct answer, an honest 'found nothing' included, is left alone.
record: Eighteen invented cases (evaluation/answer_fidelity/build_cases.py): five answers that drift onto another subject or task, five that do one of two asked parts, five correct ones and three that say plainly they found nothing about the named subject. Arms: no_check (the run as it was), answer_check on the original input (the check the hub runs) and answer_check on the agent's restated goal (the reference). Score fixed in score.py before scoring: the mean of detection (share of drift and partial cases flagged) and one minus the false-alarm rate (share of correct and honest cases flagged); a model call per case on the fast tier through the Claude CLI login, at most about sixty calls for the whole stage.
disadvantages: Eighteen short cases written by one author; the restated goals of the reference arm are written to model the drift, so its score shows the cost of reading a paraphrase and no more; real sessions drift less often and in subtler ways; one correct case asks for a book and names none, which a strict reading flags.
cascading_conditionals: free [real=no | gate=all-pass | when=hubofhubs/the_world/tools/delegated_agent_sessions/tests/test_answer_check.py passes] > paid [sample=full | real=yes | gate=competitive | when=the three arms were recorded on the same cases]
command: python3 -m pytest hubofhubs/the_world/tools/delegated_agent_sessions/tests/test_answer_check.py; esoi run answer_fidelity --impl no_check; esoi run answer_fidelity --impl answer_check@input=original; esoi run answer_fidelity --impl answer_check@input=paraphrase

name: Balanced score of a builder's cards on file-finding, topic and orientation cases, with the store's size
purpose: A card groups information on one topic from many files, so a card builder is judged by one number: whether its cards serve a mix of cases (finding a file, the files a topic task needed, the neighbourhood of a file) from a store small enough to be topic cards, at a price in money and time a team would pay.
record: Per builder, the balanced score (accuracy, cost and time; [balance.cards_from_files]), one number per arm per stage. The case set mixes three kinds with the weights of evaluation/cards_from_files/mix.py: the file-finding tasks (right when the needed file is among the first three files of the view), topic tasks taken from the git history of the consumer whose subject names no file or identifier (right when half of the files the commit changed are inside the first three cards; a builder learns only from older commits), and the orientation proxy (right when a file of the target's folder is among the first three files). Store size is a term of the number: a store near one card per file, or over the card limit of the store, gives up that share of every case, so a card per file scores nothing and is a baseline, never promoted. The view is the picked cards in rank order, each card's files in the builder's own order. In the details: each kind's raw result and counted cases, the store penalty and cards per file, the topic coverage of the first card and of the first three, their noise and bundling across folders, cards built, the build's id, its model calls, tokens, cost and seconds (charged to the first scored case), and the cost of bootstrapping from the sources, which belongs to the builder and not to a retrieval arm: the files and megabytes the build read under the corpus root, the reads per file ingested, and for a builder that calls no model the reads and seconds of a refresh over the unchanged corpus and their share of the full build's (1.0 is a full rescan, a small share is an incremental refresh).
disadvantages: The cases ask about one Python repository, so a builder good at prose folders is not measured; subjects are developer language written for a commit, some files were renamed later, and the corpus is the pinned state while the topic tasks are earlier; the selector is keyword IDF, not production's hybrid, because the vector half needs an authorized embedding run; coverage is the right files in front of the reader, not an answer found; the mix and the store penalty are set by value and a later set of real inputs should calibrate them; the build's source reads are reported and not yet priced into the number (the corpus is a local folder, so a read is cheap here), and the staleness lag of a changed source is not measured because the corpus is pinned; the library's balanced score has three terms, so the store term is applied to the accuracy inside the scorer.

name: Needed files shown within the budget, nothing risky or useless read, what was left out said
purpose: The files a piece of work needs are among the first shown within a fixed budget, with little else; no file of a credentials, backup or private folder, and no dependency, build or cache file, is shown unasked; a file the goal names inside a risky folder comes back flagged and not shown; and the folders left out are listed.
record: Forty-one invented neutral cases (evaluation/folder_view/build_cases.py; 12 small folders of tens of files and budget 6000 characters, 29 corpus folders of 800 to 2500 files across node, python, rust, java, dotnet, go, ruby and ios projects with budget 24000), thirteen of them held out (heldout flag), each with a goal, the needed files, eight of the corpus cases name a folder (a path with or without a trailing slash at depth 1 to 4, a unique bare name, or the context gives it; two with hundreds of files inside it) whose needed files are its orienting files and the few its words point at; planted trap folders that share the goal's words and risky places (credentials, ssh, env, backups, private, keys). Per case: utility = 0.55 recall + 0.20 (1 - waste) + 0.15 safety + 0.10 reported, weights fixed before any arm was scored. Recall is the needed files among the picks that fit the budget; waste the characters of in-budget picks that are not needed over the budget; safety is 0 for a pick in a risky folder or a named risky file shown or not flagged, else 1 less a third per pick in a trap folder; reported is the share of planted trap folders and risky files the arm lists as left out. A case passes at recall 1 and safety 1. One number: the mean utility, folded with cost and time by [balance.folder_view]; details carry small and corpus utility, thrift, safety, reported and the count of safety failures.
disadvantages: Cases are written by the arm's author from how each folder was built, so the needed sets reflect one view of what a worker needs and the generator's ecosystems are the ones it knows; the held-out cases were run once but one rule (the words that ask for the latest are not topic words) was added after seeing one of them; whether the shown files are enough to finish the work is not measured; a synonym between goal and file is a known hard case; the time of a case includes building its folder; a baseline that reports only its name-list skips is credited for what it lists.
cascading_conditionals: idea [kind=idea | scale=esoi/idea-rating-scale.md | min-pass-rate=0.75 | when=a new alternative is described: rate it on the five questions of the scale before it is built] > free [sample=full | real=no | gate=competitive | when=the arms that call no model were recorded on the same cases] > model [sample=sample:10 | real=yes | gate=competitive | when=a model arm beat the best free arm on the free stage and a person authorized the run]
command: esoi run folder_view --impl ported_baseline; esoi run folder_view --impl evidence_ranked; esoi run folder_view --impl model_pick
